name: Fatima Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Fatima. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Corbett's Garage on the industrial estate, and most of what we do is vans for local businesses: plumbers, the bakery's delivery vans, a couple of the council's. My day is brakes, suspension, services and a lot of fleet paperwork. I like the regulars, like the plumber who brings us cake when we turn his van round the same day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The fleet companies' online systems, where every job needs photos, codes and approval before we can start. I use the parts supplier's AI chat sometimes to find the right brake pads, and it's handy, but I check it. Gary Corbett, my boss, still writes quotes on a pad.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Danny last year, he drives lorries long distance, so he's away three nights a week. We've got a semi-detached house with a mortgage and about eight months of savings, because my dad drilled into me that you always keep a buffer. We want to start a family in two years or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds reasonable. I've never thought it would be as big as they say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like a good torque wrench, and leave it at that. At work I'd say the fleet paperwork got a bit easier. I don't really post online, maybe in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, mostly for Danny. People keep saying lorries will drive themselves, and if it all fizzles out, that's one less thing for us. My own job feels solid, because vans always need brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, and keep using the parts chat when it saves time. Stick to our plan: overpay the mortgage a little and start trying for a baby in a couple of years. And take the fleet inspection qualification Gary mentioned, so I can sign off the council vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my own work. Danny's firm is the thing at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one less thing for Danny. Is his job a worry already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. His firm lost a big contract last spring, and they cut drivers' overtime. So even without AI, I'm the steadier earner right now, which wasn't how my husband Danny and I had pictured it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would AI change at Corbett's in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fleet approvals, maybe, if the computer could fill in the forms. That's an hour a day I'd happily lose. Gary would still write his quotes on a pad, mind you.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, like a good torque wrench, and that's all.
The **fleet paperwork** at Corbett's would get a little easier.
think: She'd be **relieved for Danny**, whose lorry driving people say will be automated.
Her own job feels **solid**, because vans always need brakes.
do: Keep using the **parts supplier's AI chat** when it saves time.
Overpay the **mortgage** a little and stick to the family plan.
Take the **fleet inspection** qualification so she can sign off council vans.
feel: Her husband Danny's **shaky firm** sits at the back of her mind.
S0.quote: I'm the steadier earner right now, which wasn't how my husband Danny and I had pictured it.
fieldNote: Even with no AI shock, her household carries a **pressure**: Danny's overtime was cut.
She has become the **steadier earner**, which she didn't expect.
She uses AI **now and then** and always checks what it says.

steps.text: Keep servicing fleet vans at Corbett's Garage with the parts chat
Overpay the mortgage a little each month
Take the fleet inspection qualification to sign off council vans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels closest to what's actually coming, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the sensible thing is to learn what's proven and not jump at every new gadget. At work I'd tell Gary we should get the fleet approvals done by software, because it's already working at the big garages. In the family chat I'd tell my cousins to get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, every business with a van still needs it fixed, so a garage like Corbett's gets busier, not quieter. The office work shrinking just means Gary's daughter does the books in half the time. Danny worries me more, because route planning and dispatch are exactly the thinking jobs that go, and drivers' pay gets squeezed next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd use the AI tools the fleet companies bring in, once I've seen they work, not before. I'd keep the baby plan but save harder, a few hundred extra a month, in case Danny's hours drop. And I'd get Danny to do his forklift and warehouse tickets as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Fine for me, wobbly for the two of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until you've seen the tools work, rather than starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I watched Gary waste money on a tyre machine that broke in a month. Let someone else find the problems first. I'm not against new things, I just want them proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned telling your cousins to get a trade. Why a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad always said a trade is something nobody can take off you, and in this picture he's right for a while yet. The cousins at university doing business degrees, that's the kind of desk work this eats. I'd want them earning with their hands.

say: Learn **what's proven** and don't jump at every new gadget.
Young relatives should **get a trade** rather than a desk degree.
think: She expects Corbett's to get **busier**, because vans still need fixing.
Her husband Danny's **driving pay** looks at risk as dispatch and route planning go to AI.

Save a **few hundred extra** a month in case Danny's hours drop.
Get Danny onto **forklift and warehouse** tickets as a backup.
feel: **Uneasy**: fine for herself but **wobbly** for the household.
S1.quote: Every business with a van still needs it fixed, so a garage like Corbett's gets busier, not quieter.
fieldNote: Her caution comes from watching her boss **waste money** on a tyre machine.
She separates her **safe job** from Danny's exposed one and plans for both.
She repeats her **dad's line** that a trade is something nobody can take away.

steps.text: Use the fleet companies' AI approval tools once they're proven
Save a few hundred extra each month
Book Danny onto forklift and warehouse courses as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That's a lot faster than anyone at work thinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it won't happen like that, because things always take longer than the people selling them say. I'd say mechanics will be fine for years. I'd probably believe about half of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the dispatch and planning side of Danny's work goes in 2028, and self-driving lorries are robots of a sort, so 2031 for him at the latest. Mine goes around 2031 too, when I'm 32. My husband and I losing our work in the same three years is the bit that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the baby plan on hold until I know where our money is coming from. I'd want us to throw everything at the mortgage for two years. And I'd start looking at what the robot garages would still need, an inspector or a manager, someone people trust to sign off their van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the both-of-us part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting the baby plan on hold, how would that conversation go with Danny?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. His mum asks every Sunday when she's getting a grandchild. But Danny's practical, he'd see that having a baby the year we both lose our wages isn't fair on the baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on anyone, family or government, if it got bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, always. My parents have a bit put away and they've said the door's open. I wouldn't want government money unless there was no other way, that's how I was brought up.

say: It won't happen that fast, because things **always take longer** than sellers say.
Mechanics will be **fine for years**, though she only half believes it.
think: Danny's driving work goes when AI and **self-driving lorries** arrive, by 2031.
Her own repair work goes **around 2031** too, when she's 32.
do: Put the **baby plan** on hold until the household income is clear.
Throw everything at the **mortgage** for two years.
Look for a **van inspector** or manager role that robot garages would still need.
feel: **Alarmed**, because both household earners could lose their work together.
S2.quote: My husband and I losing our work in the same three years is the bit that scares me.
fieldNote: The **double exposure** of her and Danny is what moves her from uneasy to alarmed.
She'd turn to **family before government**, as she was brought up to.
She looks for a **trust role**, signing off vans, that robots might not fill.

steps.text: Put trying for a baby on hold until income is settled
Throw every spare bit of pay at the mortgage for two years
Accept her parents' offer of help if both wages go
Look for van inspector or garage manager roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get their house in order, literally, while they can. At work I'd tell Gary the garage should be the trusted local name before the robot chains turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots in 2034 means I've got about eight years of hands-on work, and I'd be 35. Danny's lorry work goes sooner, with the planning side hit by 2031. Eight years is enough to have our first baby and get the mortgage well down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the baby plan, maybe even bring it forward a year, so the kids are older by the time things change. I'd get the fleet inspection qualification this year, and then aim for the manager's job when Gary retires. Danny would start retraining now, maybe as an electrician, on evening courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels manageable. There's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bringing the baby forward seems the opposite of what you'd do with two years. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with five years I'd rather have the little one while both our wages are still solid. Two years is too close for a baby, but eight years is a window. My mum had me when she was 28, and that feels right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Danny feel about retraining as an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, he likes the open road and the quiet. But his brother's an electrician and does well. He'd come round once he saw the numbers.

say: People should get their **house in order** while they can.
Corbett's should be the **trusted local name** before robot chains arrive.
think: Robots by **2034** leave her about eight years of hands-on work.
Danny's lorry work **goes sooner**, with planning hit by 2031.
do: Keep the **baby plan**, maybe bringing it forward a year.
Get the **fleet inspection** qualification and aim for manager when Gary retires.
Get Danny onto **evening electrician** courses now.
S3.quote: Two years is too close for a baby, but eight years is a window.
fieldNote: She **flips** her family plan: with more time she brings the baby forward.
She bets on **trust and sign-off** roles as the last human part of the garage.
She plans **Danny's retraining** as firmly as her own career.

steps.text: Try for a first baby a year earlier than planned
Pass the fleet inspection qualification this year
Sign Danny up for evening electrician courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time enough for anyone who's willing to work, and I wouldn't have much patience for people who waste it. At family dinners I'd say the same to my younger brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the comfortable one. Robots in 2039 means I'm 40, the kids would be at school and the mortgage nearly done. The thing I'd watch is the AI side changing the garage earlier, the bookings and quotes, because that's 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, nothing dramatic: work, save, have our first baby on schedule. I'd get my inspection qualification and maybe a management course at the college. I'd keep an eye on the big chains and only move when I see robots actually working on cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't have much patience for people who waste the decade. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother Sami, if I'm honest. He's 22, works in a call centre and says it'll all sort itself out. In this picture his job goes first, and he's got ten years' warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sami?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade, like Dad told both of us. Or at least learn to do something with your hands while the AI does the phone calls. I'd pay for my brother's first course if he'd actually turn up.

She'd have little **patience** for people who waste it.

She'd watch for AI in **bookings and quotes**, which arrives sooner in 2036.

Take the inspection qualification and a **management course** at the college.

fieldNote: Ten years lets her **wait for proof**, which matches how she handles change.
Her worry shifts to her brother Sami, whose **call centre** job goes first.
She'd **pay for a course** for him, but only if he commits.

steps.text: Keep working at Corbett's and have the first baby as planned
Take a management course at the local college
Hold off any job move until robots are seen fixing cars

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's me and Danny at once, and maybe a baby on the way if we'd already started. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay a proper wage while you learn, like the one I had at 17. And firms giving their people a few years' notice instead of telling them on a Monday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the families. Everyone talks about jobs, but it's whether you can have a child and keep a roof over them. My dad always said a family needs one solid wage and one backup, and AI could take both.

headlineQuote: My dad always said a family needs one solid wage and one backup, and AI could take both.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old mechanic servicing **fleet vans** at Corbett's Garage on an industrial estate.
She's married to Danny, a **lorry driver** whose firm has already cut overtime.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts new tools only once they're proven.
In the fast AGI picture the **double exposure** of both wages makes her pause the baby plan.
With more warning she brings the **baby forward** and plans Danny's retraining alongside her own.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Danny could lose both wages at once.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **adult apprenticeships** that let people learn on a proper wage.
Firms giving workers **years of notice** instead of sudden news.
